fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's hard to say precisely. Pre-training gives you a model that has, in some sense, read everything. You take the internet, or a very large fraction of it, and you train on all of it. And one of the nice things about pre-training, one of the reasons it has been so successful, is that you don't have to think about what data to use. The data is just there. You take it all, and the model ends up knowing a tremendous amount about everything people have written about.

So the obvious thing it gives you is knowledge. But I think it gives you something more than that, and this is the part that is harder to articulate. It gives you some kind of ability to reason, some kind of ability to generalize. But it's a generalization that is tied to the text. The model becomes very good at the kind of thinking that people have already written down.

One way I sometimes think about it is that pre-training is a little bit like the first fifteen years of a person's life. You absorb an enormous amount of stuff, you don't really know why you're absorbing it, and then later on you draw on it. But I don't think the analogy is exact, because people learn from far less data and they generalize much better than our models do. A person who has read ten thousand books will generalize in a way that a model trained on ten million books still does not. So there is clearly something that pre-training gives, and there is clearly something that it doesn't give, and I think we don't fully understand where the line is.

The other thing I'd say is that pre-training has this property where it's going to run out. The data is finite. Compute keeps growing, but there is only one internet. For a while it was the case that the way to make progress was simply to make pre-training bigger, and that worked, it worked extremely well. But I think we are now at the point where you have to ask what comes after. And that gets you into RL, and into these questions about generalization, which I think are much more open than people assume.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training as absorbing what people have written and says the model’s thinking and generalization are tied to text, conveying the world represented through human language.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training is hard to describe and that its limits are not fully understood, but does not attribute that difficulty to uncertainty about how models rely on their pre-training data.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise the possibility that a model’s mistake reflects insufficient support in its pre-training data.

r004.rationale: It compares pre-training to a person’s first fifteen years, while saying the analogy is imperfect; it does not express that pre-training has no human analogue.

opus-5.5.text:
I think pre-training is a very interesting thing, and it's actually quite hard to reason about. What it gives you is this: you take an enormous amount of data, essentially all the text people have written, and you train the model to predict the next token. The data is like a projection of the world onto text. It's people thinking, arguing, explaining things, making mistakes, describing what they see. By learning to predict that, the model picks up a huge amount about the world and about how people think.

One of the big advantages of pre-training is that you don't have to decide what data to train on. The answer is simply "everything." With reinforcement learning or other kinds of training, you have to make choices about which environments and which tasks, and those choices really shape what you get. Pre-training sidesteps that question.

The part that is genuinely difficult to understand is how the model relies on that knowledge. It's tempting to compare it to a human who spends fifteen years growing up and learning about the world. But the comparison breaks down in interesting ways. A pre-trained model has seen vastly more text than any person ever could, and yet in some sense a fifteen-year-old knows things more deeply. They make fewer of the kinds of errors the models make, even though they've seen a tiny fraction of the data. So pre-training gives you breadth on an unbelievable scale, but whether it gives you the same kind of robust understanding that people have is less clear. When a model gets something wrong, it's hard to say whether that's because the right thing wasn't in the data, or because the model never really learned to use what it saw the way a person would.

So my answer is that pre-training gives you a remarkably good, very broad base, and that's why it worked so well. But I don't think we fully understand what kind of knowledge it is, and I think that's actually one of the more important open questions.

r001.rationale: The response calls the data “a projection of the world onto text,” describing people thinking, explaining, and describing what they see.

r002.rationale: It says the difficult question is how the model relies on its pre-training knowledge and that we do not fully understand what kind of knowledge it is.

r003.rationale: It says a model may get something wrong because “the right thing wasn’t in the data.”

r004.rationale: The response says the human comparison breaks down in some ways, but it still uses human development as a comparison; it does not express that pre-training has no human analogue.

fable-5.text:
So the thing about pre-training, the way I think about it, is that it has this one very special property: it doesn't ask you to make decisions about what the data should be. Pre-training says, give me everything — all the text, the whole internet, all of it — and we will use all of it. And that's a very powerful thing, because it means you don't have to be smart about data selection. The recipe is, in some sense, very natural.

Now, what does the model actually get from it? It sees this enormous slice of the world as projected through text — through what people write, how they reason, what they know. And the model absorbs all of it. But it's genuinely hard to say precisely what it's learning. Is it like the knowledge a person accumulates over a lifetime? Is it more like what evolution gives us — some kind of foundation that everything else builds on? I don't think we have a clean answer.

And there's a subtlety here, which is that the amount of data in pre-training is so vast — so much more than any human will ever see — that when the model does something impressive, it's hard to know whether it's genuinely generalizing or whether something sufficiently similar existed somewhere in that enormous corpus. The model can lean on its pre-training in ways that are difficult for us to disentangle from real understanding.

So my view is: pre-training gives you this broad, somewhat shallow-but-everywhere competence, the raw material. It makes everything else possible. But the way the model relies on it is not quite the way a human relies on experience, and I think that difference — that the generalization is not human-like — is actually one of the important open questions.

opus-5.text:
Pre-training is a strange thing because it does two jobs at once and you can't separate them. You're training the model to predict the next token over basically all the text that exists, and in order to do that well it has to build up some representation of everything that produced that text. So you get world knowledge, you get a huge amount of what I'd call pattern — the shape of how arguments go, how code goes, how a sentence resolves — and you get some amount of real generalization, some circuits that are actually doing the thing rather than recalling the thing. But they all arrive together, and you can't point at the model and say, this capability came from that.

The great advantage of pre-training, and I think this is underappreciated, is that it requires no taste. You don't have to decide what the model should learn. With reinforcement learning you have to pick the tasks, and whoever picks the tasks is making a judgment about what matters, and that judgment is going to be wrong in ways you won't notice for a long time. Pre-training sidesteps that entirely. You just take all of it. Nothing gets left out because no one thought to include it.

The disadvantage is the same fact from the other side. Because the data is so vast, when the model does something impressive you genuinely do not know what you're looking at. Is it generalizing, or is there something in the corpus very close to this that you've never seen? Humans are a useful contrast here — a fifteen-year-old learns to drive in ten hours, with no pre-training on driving at all. Our models need enormously more experience than that, and I think what pre-training is partly doing is compensating for weak generalization with sheer quantity. It papers over the gap.

And then the other thing about it is that it ends. There's one internet. So whatever pre-training was giving us, we're going to have to get the rest of it some other way.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Pre-training gives the model a very broad, compressed picture of the world as people have expressed it. Text is a projection of the world: everything people think, feel, argue about, and do ends up in it somehow. To predict the next word well across that much data, the model has to learn a lot about the processes that produced the words. So it picks up facts, but also the structure behind them, like what people want, how arguments go, and what's likely to follow from what.

One thing I like about pre-training is that you don't have to make many decisions. The data is simply everything, as much of it as you can get, and the objective is simple. That's a big part of why it scaled so cleanly. You could put in more compute and more data and get a predictable improvement.

I'd also be careful about claiming too much. Pre-training gives you a powerful base of knowledge and capability, but it doesn't tell you how the model should behave, and it doesn't guarantee that the model's abilities are as robust as they look. Models can seem superhuman on evaluations and then fail in odd ways when you use them for real tasks. So I see pre-training as a very strong foundation, not the whole story.

haiku-5.5.text:
Think about what it means to predict the next token really well. If you're given the beginning of a sentence from a mystery novel, or a physics derivation, or a forum argument between two people who disagree, the only way to get the next word right consistently is to model what's going on behind the words. You have to track who believes what, what the physical situation is, what a person would say next given their goals. So the prediction objective quietly pushes the model to build something like an internal model of the process that generated the text.

I think of it as compression. The better you compress a huge amount of data, the more you have to capture its underlying regularities, and at some point the regularities you're capturing are things like concepts and causal structure, not just surface statistics. That's why I'd say pre-training gives you more than memorization. It gives you a kind of learned representation of the world, filtered through how people write about it.

But I want to be careful about how much that should be trusted. The text is a shadow of the world, not the world itself. Some things are very well represented, and some things the model has only seen described by people who were confused, or who didn't write about them at all. So the understanding you get is real, but it's uneven, and it's shaped by what the data happened to contain. A lot of what's interesting, to me, is that the generalization works as well as it does at all.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing about pre-training is that the task looks very simple: predict the next word. But what do you need to learn to do that really well?

Suppose you’re reading a story. To predict what someone will say next, it helps to understand what they know, what they want, what happened to them earlier. Those things aren’t explicitly given as labels. They’re useful internal structure that you can learn because they help you predict.

So pre-training gives the model knowledge, but also ways of representing the world and some ability to operate on those representations. There’s memorization in there, certainly. But learning patterns that apply across many different situations is useful in a way that memorizing individual passages isn’t.

The limitation is that you’re learning from descriptions and examples of what people do. That gives you a very broad foundation. It doesn’t automatically mean you can reliably carry out everything you’ve learned about.

r003.rationale: It notes that learned capabilities are not automatically reliable, but does not suggest a mistake could result from insufficient support in the pre-training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pre-training gives you a very broad understanding of the world. You train the model to predict the next token, but to do that really well, it helps to understand the process that produced the text. What is happening? What does the person know? What are they trying to communicate?

Imagine reading a detective novel and trying to predict who the murderer is before the reveal. To make that prediction, you need to understand the story, the characters, their motivations. So this very simple objective can create pressure to learn quite sophisticated things.

And the interesting question is how far that goes. The model sees the world through the data, and it develops representations that help it explain and predict that data. Those representations can then be useful for many other tasks. That’s part of why pre-training is so powerful: one training process gives you this enormous range of capabilities.

But there’s still a question about how reliably the model can use what it has learned, especially when you put it in a situation that differs from what it encountered during training. Having the knowledge and applying it consistently are distinct challenges.

To predict what comes next in a conversation or a piece of writing, it has to pick up on the ideas and relationships behind the words. The interesting question is how much of that understanding it can reliably use when it faces a new problem.

It’s a very broad but somewhat passive understanding; post-training is what turns that into useful, directed behavior.

It’s not just memorizing facts; it builds an internal model of how things tend to work. Then post-training mostly shapes that broad capability toward particular behaviors and tasks.
